entries.narration: Imagine a shop that wants the total for an order. In plain words: take the price of one item, multiply it by how many were ordered, and show the answer. That list of three steps, at the top of the diagram, is an algorithm. It says what to do, it is not tied to any language, and a person could follow it with a pencil. Now we write those steps down in Python. What we write is called source code, and it is just ordinary text, saved in a file whose name ends in dot py. Here it is in three lines: price is four point five, quantity is three, and print the product. But a computer's processor cannot read Python text directly. So another program, called the interpreter, reads our source code and carries out each instruction. One instruction is called a statement, and the interpreter works through them in order. What it produces comes out as output, here on the screen, as thirteen point five. A program can also read input from outside, such as a quantity typed by a person, and we will meet that shortly. Throughout this course, the interpreter we mean is CPython, the standard one, at version three point fourteen. The important habit to take from this first section is that the interpreter does exactly what the text says. It never guesses what you meant. And because the algorithm is separate from the code, the same three steps could be written in many other languages. That is why the algorithm comes first and the code second, and it is why we will spend so much time tracing what each line really does. Next, we will run this order total for real, in two different ways.

Python can run your code in two ways, and the difference trips up almost every beginner. The first is an interactive session. You see a prompt made of three greater-than signs, you type one statement, and Python runs it immediately. If the statement is an expression, meaning something that produces a value, Python shows you that value straight away. That makes a session ideal for trying an idea or checking a result. The second way is a script. You save your statements in a file, here called order dot py, and ask Python to run the whole file from the top to the bottom. A script is the right choice for a program you want to keep and run again. Let us trace the script on screen, one line at a time. Line one gives the name price the value four. Line two gives the name quantity the value three. Line three multiplies them and gets twelve, and then nothing happens to that twelve. A script does not echo values the way a session does, so the result is calculated and then simply thrown away. Only line four, which calls print, puts anything on the screen. You can see that in the terminal card: the whole run shows a single twelve. So the same expression, price times quantity, displays twelve in a session but displays nothing in a script. If a script is supposed to show an answer, it has to say so, with print. The commands you see are illustrations, and you are welcome to try them, but you do not need to in order to follow along.

Here is the most important picture in this course. In Python, a value is an object that lives in memory, and a name is only a label that refers to an object. The diagram has names on the left and objects on the right. When we write price equals four point five, we do not put the number inside price. We create a float object holding four point five, and we make the name price refer to it. The equals sign here is called assignment. It binds a name to an object. It does not claim that two things are equal, the way it does in arithmetic. Every object has a type, and the five you will meet first are shown with the objects. An int is a whole number, like three. A float is a number with a decimal point, like four point five. A str, short for string, is text, written between quotes, like tea. A bool is either True or False. And None is a special object that means there is deliberately no value, here for a coupon that was not supplied. You can ask any object for its type by calling type on the name that refers to it. Notice that the type belongs to the object, not to the name. A name can be rebound. If we later write price equals five point zero, the name price now refers to a different object, and the old four point five is left untouched. Finally, a few rules for choosing names. A name is made of letters, digits, and underscores, and it cannot start with a digit. Case matters, so price with a lowercase p and Price with a capital P are two different names. Keep this picture of names pointing at objects in mind, because chapters ahead will extend it rather than replace it.

An expression is any piece of code that produces a value, and the table shows ten of them with exactly what Python produces. Start with division, which comes in three forms. The single slash always gives a float, so seven divided by two is three point five, and even ten divided by two is five point zero, with a decimal point. The double slash divides and rounds down to a whole number, so seven double-slash two is three. Rounding down means toward minus infinity, so minus seven double-slash two is minus four, not minus three. The percent sign gives the remainder, so seven percent two is one. Double asterisk is the power, so two to the tenth is one thousand and twenty-four. When an expression has several operators, Python applies power first, then multiplication and division together, then addition and subtraction, and you can use parentheses to force a different order. Now the numbers themselves. An int is exact at any size: two to the hundredth power is a thirty-one digit number, with no overflow, limited only by memory. A float is different. Zero point one plus zero point two does not give zero point three. It gives zero point three followed by a long tail of zeros and a four. A float stores the nearest value it can represent in binary, and many decimal fractions simply have no exact binary form. This is not a bug in Python. On CPython, a float is a sixty-four bit binary floating-point number, and any language using that representation behaves the same way. That is also why comparing the sum to zero point three with a double equals gives False, so you should be careful comparing floats when the decimals matter. Finally, converting between types is something you ask for. Calling int on three point nine gives three, because it cuts off the decimal part rather than rounding. And calling float on the text two point five gives the number two point five. When money is involved, we will need something safer than float, and we will meet it later in the course.

Now the complete order-total program, with its input and its output. Read it top to bottom with me. Line one calls input with the prompt Quantity. Python shows that prompt, waits, and returns whatever the person typed. The crucial fact is that input always returns a str, a piece of text, even when the person typed digits. So after line one, the name text refers to the text three, not the number three. Line two fixes that by calling int on it, which converts the text into the whole number three. Line three gives price the float four point five. Line four multiplies, giving thirteen point five. Line five prints the answer using an f-string. An f-string is a string with the letter f in front of the opening quote, and anything inside curly braces is replaced by its value. After the value comes a colon and a format. Dot two f means a float with exactly two digits after the decimal point, so thirteen point five prints as thirteen point five zero. Adding a greater-than sign and a width, as in eight dot two f, also right-aligns the number in a field eight characters wide. The terminal card shows one run, where the person typed three. Now the failure that makes this section worth learning, shown in the last card. If we skip the int conversion, then three as text, multiplied by two, does not give six. It gives the text three, three, because multiplying text repeats it. And adding the number one to that text is rejected with a TypeError, because Python will not mix text and numbers. Conversion can fail too: asking int to convert the text three point five raises a ValueError, because that text is not a whole number. The lesson is to always know whether a name refers to text or to a number, and to convert at the boundary where text comes in.

Programs fail, and a beginner's best skill is telling the three kinds of failure apart, so the diagram gives one worked example of each. The first is a syntax error. The text is not valid Python, so Python refuses to run any of it. For example, print with a string followed directly by a number, with no comma between them, is rejected, and Python even suggests that you might have forgotten a comma. The second is a runtime error. The text is valid, the program starts, and then one statement fails while running. Python stops and prints a traceback, which is the report on screen. Read a traceback from the bottom. The last line gives the type of the error and a message, here a ValueError, saying that the text three is not a valid whole number. The lines above show where it happened: the file order dot py, line two, and the code on that line, quantity equals int of text. If the failing call was made from inside other code, there would be more lines, and the one nearest the bottom is the closest to the failure. The exact wording of messages can differ a little between Python versions, but the shape is always the same. The third kind is the hardest, because there is no message at all. If we write price plus quantity instead of price times quantity, Python happily gives seven point five, which is wrong for our order. Only careful tracing, checking results against what you expect, can catch that. A few error names will turn up again and again. A NameError means a name has no object yet, usually because of a typo. A TypeError means an operation was applied to the wrong kind of object. A ValueError means the type was right but the value was not acceptable. And a ZeroDivisionError means exactly what it says. And that is the end of our first chapter. One order can now be represented by a handful of values. Next, we turn to organising many related values and many orders, with strings, lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets.

Our order system identifies each product with a code, like tea dash two fifty g. A string is more than a blob of text. It is an ordered sequence of characters, and the table shows exactly that: one column per character, each with a position. Python counts positions from zero, so the first character, t, is at index zero, and the last, g, is at index seven. You can also count from the end using negative numbers, so index minus one is always the last character. Ask for an index that does not exist and Python raises an IndexError. Slicing takes a piece of the string. You write start, a colon, and stop, and the slice includes the start position but excludes the stop position. So the slice from the beginning up to three gives t, e, a, which is tea, and the slice from four onwards gives two fifty g. You can leave either end out, and unlike a single index, a slice that runs past the end does not fail, it just gives what is there, even an empty string. Adding a second colon and a step of minus one walks backwards, which reverses the string. Strings also come with methods, which are operations you call with a dot. Upper makes capitals, and split cuts the string wherever it finds a separator and gives back a list. The key point is that every one of these returns a new string. Strings are immutable, meaning an existing string can never be changed in place. Trying to assign a new letter to position zero raises a TypeError. Lists, which come next, behave very differently.

A list is Python's everyday collection. It holds items in order, written between square brackets, and unlike a string, it can change after it is created. Indexing and slicing work exactly as they did for strings, so items at index one is the second item, and a slice gives back a new list. The code card traces a list of ordered items through several changes. Append adds an item at the end. Assigning to an index replaces the item at that position. Pop removes the last item and hands it back to us, here the jar. Insert places a new item at a chosen position, here at the front. We can also ask questions: count tells us how many times tea appears, and index tells us where cup is. Notice that all of these changes happen to the same list object. Nothing new is created, and that is what mutable means. Now look at the table, because it holds the most common list mistake. Append, insert, remove and sort all change the list, and all of them return None, nothing at all. So if you write items equals items dot sort, you have just thrown your list away and replaced it with None. When you want a new, sorted list and want to leave the original alone, use the sorted function instead, which returns a brand new list. Finally, plus joins two lists into a new list, and multiplying a list by a number repeats it. Next, a collection that deliberately refuses to change.

A tuple looks like a list written with parentheses, and it supports the same indexing and slicing. The difference is that a tuple can never change after it is created. That sounds like a limitation, but it is what makes a tuple useful as a record. In the code card, the order is a tuple of an id, an item, a quantity and a price. Each position is a field with its own meaning, and because the tuple cannot change, the meaning of each position cannot be disturbed by accident. Trying to assign a new quantity raises a TypeError. There is one small piece of syntax to remember. A tuple with a single item needs a trailing comma. Three followed by a comma is a tuple holding one number, but three in plain parentheses is just the number three, because parentheses also group expressions. Immutability has a second benefit. Dictionaries, which we meet next, need keys that can never change underneath them. A tuple qualifies, so an order tuple can be used as a key. A list does not, and Python reports that a list is unhashable. The table sums up the choice. Use a list for many alike items that may grow or shrink, and a tuple for a few fields that belong together as one thing. One subtlety: a tuple itself cannot change, but if one of its items is a list, that list can still be changed. The tuple only guarantees which objects it holds.

When fields have names, a dictionary is the natural shape. A dictionary maps keys to values, and you look something up by its key rather than by its position. Our order is now a dictionary with the keys id, item, and qty. Reading a value uses square brackets with the key. Assigning to an existing key updates it, and assigning to a new key adds it, so the same syntax does both. Pop removes a key and returns the value that was stored. The list and values calls on the card show the keys and values in the order they were inserted. Since Python three point seven, that insertion order is guaranteed, so a dictionary remembers the order in which you built it. Now the table, which is about a failure you will meet constantly. If you ask for a key that is not there using square brackets, Python raises a KeyError. That is often correct, because a missing field may be a real bug. But when a missing key is normal, use the get method. Get returns None if the key is absent, and if you pass a second argument, it returns that instead, as a default. And the in operator asks whether a key exists without fetching anything. One rule about keys: they must be hashable, which in practice means strings, numbers, and tuples of those, but not lists. Next, a collection that keeps only the keys.

A set is a collection with two defining properties: it has no duplicates, and it has no order. You write one with curly braces, such as tea, mug, and jar. An empty set is the exception, because empty curly braces make an empty dictionary, so an empty set must be written as set with parentheses. Turning a list into a set removes duplicates, so the list with tea twice becomes a set of length two. Checking whether something is in a set is fast, which makes sets the right tool for membership questions. The real power is the operators, shown in the table for two sets: what we ordered, and what is in stock. The bar gives the union, everything in either set. The ampersand gives the intersection, the items in both. Minus gives the difference, so ordered minus in stock tells us what we ordered but cannot supply. And the caret gives items in exactly one of the two. Notice that every result in the table is wrapped in sorted. That is deliberate. A set has no order, so there is no index, and the order in which a set of strings prints can even differ from one run of the program to the next. If you need a stable display, sort it. As with dictionary keys, items must be hashable, so a set cannot contain a list. To drop duplicates and keep a stable order, write sorted of set of codes. Use a set when the question is membership or uniqueness, and a list when order matters.

This is the most important idea in the chapter, and it is the name-and-object picture from Chapter 1 doing real work. Read the code card. The name a refers to a list. Then b equals a does not create a second list. It creates a second name for the very same list. Next, c equals a dot copy creates a genuinely new list that happens to hold the same items. The diagram shows the result after we append four through the name b. The names a and b both reach the changed list, which now holds four items. The name c still reaches the separate copy, unchanged. This is called aliasing, and it explains many surprises: changing a list through one name changes it for every name that refers to it. Python gives you two different questions to ask. Double equals asks whether two objects hold the same contents, and is asks whether they are literally the same object. The copy is equal to the original, which prints True, but it is not the original, which prints False. Now a subtler trap. Copy, and slicing with colon, make a shallow copy, which copies only the outer list. If the list contains other lists, those inner lists are still shared. So appending nine to an inner list of the copy changes the original as well. When you need every level copied, the copy module provides deepcopy. Finally, strings, numbers and tuples cannot be changed, so sharing them is harmless. The danger is specific to mutable objects.

Real data is rarely a single flat collection, so this section puts the pieces together. First, unpacking. When you write three names on the left of an equals sign and a three-item sequence on the right, Python binds each name to the matching item. So oid, item, and qty receive the id, the item, and the quantity from the order. The counts must match: unpacking three items into two names raises a ValueError saying there were too many values. A name with a star in front collects whatever is left into a list, so first, star rest, on ten, twenty, thirty gives ten, and a rest of twenty and thirty. The last line of that group shows a neat idiom: writing x, y equals y, x swaps two names in one statement. Second, nested collections. Our orders are a list of dictionaries, each holding a list of line tuples. To read the name of the second line of the first order, you move one level at a time: the first order, then its lines, then the second line, then the first field. Each pair of brackets goes one level deeper. And in a loop you can unpack each line directly into a name, a quantity and a price. The table compares the four shapes you now know. Nesting has its own failures, and each one is a lesson from earlier: an index past the end of a list raises an IndexError, and an absent key raises a KeyError, so read nested data one level at a time and you can tell which level failed. Pick a tuple for fixed fields by position, a dictionary for named fields, and a list of records for many rows that share a shape. Next, we sort and summarise.

Once data is in a collection, you often want to summarise or reorder it. The table shows the built-in functions for summarising a list of prices. Len gives the count, sum adds the numbers, and min and max find the smallest and largest. Reversed walks a list backwards, and wrapping it in list gives the reversed items. Now sorting, in the code card. The sorted function returns a new list in ascending order and leaves the original alone. Passing reverse equals True flips the order. Sorting needs items that can be compared, so a list mixing a number and a string raises a TypeError. The interesting part is the key argument. By default, Python compares the items themselves, but with a key, it applies a function to each item first and orders by the result. Sorting the words by len puts the shortest first. Notice that pear and kiwi both have four letters, and they stay in their original order, pear before kiwi. That is because Python's sort is stable, so ties never get shuffled. Another useful key is str dot lower, which ignores capital letters when comparing. Without it, all capitals sort before all lowercase letters, which is surprising. For now we use only functions that already exist. In Chapter 4, you will write your own key function, and then you can sort orders by their total.

We end the chapter with a first look at comprehensions, so that you can recognise one when you see it. Start with the loop on top. We have a list of lines, each a quantity and a price. We make an empty list, then repeat for each line, and append the quantity times the price. The result is thirteen point five, eight, and four point five. A comprehension says the same thing in a single expression. In square brackets, you write the value you want, then for, then the name or names to take from the collection, then in, then the collection. Read it aloud: for each quantity and price in lines, produce quantity times price. If you add if and a condition at the end, only matching items are kept, so adding if qty is greater than one leaves just the first and last totals. The brackets decide what gets built. Square brackets build a list. Curly braces with a key, a colon and a value build a dictionary, as with each name mapped to its length. Curly braces with just a value build a set, so the set of lengths for tea, mug and jar is just three, because duplicates collapse. We have only previewed the idea. Chapter 3 explains how loops and filters actually run, and then comprehensions will make complete sense. And if a transformation has several steps or side effects, a plain loop is usually clearer. We now have data structures. Next, we explain how decisions and iteration transform their contents.

Every decision a program makes rests on a condition, which is an expression that Python can treat as true or false. The simplest conditions are comparisons. Double equals asks whether two values are equal, exclamation equals asks whether they differ, and the four angle-bracket operators compare size. Each gives back True or False. They can also be chained, so zero less than qty less than or equal to five checks both ends at once. Be careful with one thing: a single equals sign assigns a name, and a double equals compares, and swapping them is a classic mistake. Python does not insist on a True or False. Any value can be used as a condition, and it counts as true or false by a simple rule. Zero, an empty string, an empty list, an empty dictionary, and None all count as false. Everything else counts as true, which includes the text zero and the text False, because non-empty text is non-empty text. The table shows seven examples. Next, the Boolean operators. And, or, and not combine conditions. There is a subtle detail: and and or do not always return True or False. They return one of the operands. Coupon or the text no coupon gives the text, because coupon is None, which is false. And qty and price gives four point five, the last operand it looked at. Finally, they short-circuit, meaning the right-hand side is evaluated only if the left side has not already decided the answer. That is why the last line is safe. When qty is zero, the left side is False, so Python never evaluates the division, and there is no ZeroDivisionError. Next, using conditions to choose between blocks of code.

A decision lets a program choose which code to run. The statement is if, followed by a condition and a colon. The lines indented beneath it form a block, and the block runs only if the condition is true. Indentation is how Python knows which lines belong together, so it is part of the syntax, not decoration. In our shipping example, we add elif, short for else if, to test a second condition, and else, to catch everything that matched nothing. Python tests the conditions from the top and runs only the first branch whose condition is true, then skips the rest. The table traces five totals. Sixty and fifty both run the first branch, because greater-than-or-equal includes the boundary value, fifty. Twenty-five and twenty run the elif. And thirteen point five matches neither test, so the else runs and the shipping is five. That is the final line of the code card. Order matters, and this is a real bug, not a matter of style. If we had written the greater-than-or-equal-twenty test first, a total of sixty would match it immediately and be charged two point five, and the fifty test would never be reached. Always test the narrowest case first. Decisions can also be nested, with an if inside a branch of another if, which refines that branch. When there is no separate else for the inner question, joining the two conditions with and is often clearer. Two mistakes to recognise: a missing indent raises an IndentationError, and writing a single equals sign in a condition is a SyntaxError, and Python even suggests double equals.

A loop repeats a block of code. The for loop is the loop for working through a collection: it takes one item at a time from something iterable, which means anything you can step through, such as a list, a string, a tuple, a dictionary's keys, or a set. In our example, for price in prices binds the name price to the first item, runs the indented block, then binds it to the second item, and so on, until the items run out. Each run through the block is called a pass. The table traces the loop state after each pass, and learning to fill in a table like this is the best way to understand any loop. Before the loop, total is zero. After the first pass it is four point five, after the second twelve point five, and after the third fourteen point seven five, which is what we print. This pattern, starting a value before the loop and updating it inside, is called accumulating. One detail: after the loop ends, the name price still refers to its last value. Now the helpers in the second card. Range produces a sequence of whole numbers. Range of three gives zero, one, two, because the stop value is excluded, just as with slices. Adding a start and a step, range of one to six by two gives one, three, five. Enumerate pairs a counter with each item, and giving it a start of one numbers the items from one. And zip walks two collections together, pairing the first with the first and the second with the second, and stopping when the shorter one runs out. Next, a loop that repeats until a condition changes.

A while loop repeats a block for as long as its condition stays true. Unlike a for loop, it is not tied to a collection. The condition is tested before every pass, including the first, so if it is false from the start, the body never runs at all. Our example fills orders from a stock of one hundred, thirty units at a time. The table traces it. On the first pass, stock is one hundred, the test is True, and after the body, stock is seventy and one order is filled. The second pass tests seventy, True, and leaves forty. The third tests forty, True, and leaves ten. On the fourth test, ten is not at least thirty, so the test is False and the loop ends. That last row is easy to forget: the test always runs one more time than the body. We print three orders filled and ten units left. A while loop carries a risk that a for loop does not: it can run forever. The last card shows the shape. If the body never changes n, the condition n greater than zero stays true forever, and the program prints five endlessly. The rule is that the body must make progress, meaning something in it must move the condition toward false. If you ever start such a loop by accident, Control-C interrupts it. Boundaries need care too. With greater-than-or-equal thirty, a stock of exactly thirty gets a final pass, and with plain greater-than it does not. When you trace a loop, check the first pass, a middle one, and the last. As a rule of thumb, use for when you have a collection or a known count, and while when you repeat until something changes.

Two statements change how a loop runs. Break ends the loop immediately, and continue skips the rest of the current pass and moves on to the next one. The first example searches a list of codes. When code equals B dash two, we print found and break, and the loop stops, so C dash three is never examined. Notice the else block attached to the for loop. Else after a loop runs only if the loop finished without hitting break. Here we found the code, so the else is skipped. If we had searched for a code that is not in the list, the loop would run to the end, and the else would print not found. Read it as: if we never found it. The second example uses continue. For the quantities three, zero, and two, we want one hundred divided by each quantity. When the quantity is zero, continue skips the division, so there is no ZeroDivisionError, and we get thirty-three point three, repeating, and then fifty. Now the table of common mistakes. The subtlest is changing a list while looping over it. If you remove the even numbers from the list two, four, six inside a for loop, the loop skips items as the list shrinks beneath it, and the result is a list with four still in it. The safe pattern is to build a new list with a comprehension. The other mistakes you have already met: a while loop with no progress never ends, looping over range of len of x when you could loop over x directly makes the code clumsy, and a single equals in a condition is a SyntaxError.

So far, decisions have compared values. Structural pattern matching, added in Python three point ten, does something different: it compares the shape of a value. The code card matches an order, which is a dictionary. Python tries each case from the top and runs the first one that fits. The first pattern requires the item to be tea and the quantity to be exactly zero, and our order does not fit. The second requires tea and any quantity, and it does fit, and notice what happens to the name q: it captures the value three, so we can use it in the body, and status becomes three tea. The third case would match any order with an item, and the underscore case matches anything at all, as a final fallback. The table lists the pattern kinds. A literal like the text tea matches that exact value. A bare name matches anything and binds it. The underscore matches anything and binds nothing. A tuple pattern matches a sequence of that shape, and a dictionary pattern matches any dictionary with those keys. This is where match differs from ordinary comparison, and it has two traps. First, a bare name in a case does not compare against a variable. Writing case tea would capture whatever was passed into a new name tea, matching everything. Only literals compare. Second, you can add a guard with if, and you can combine alternatives with a bar, but a guard runs on whatever matched, so a guard comparing greater than one hundred would raise a TypeError on text. Check the type first. For plain comparisons, if and elif remain the right tool.

This section turns the loops you can now trace into small algorithms. The first is aggregation. We have three sales lines, and we want a total per item. We start with an empty dictionary. For each line, we unpack the item, quantity, and price, then add the line total to whatever the dictionary already holds for that item. The call to get with a default of zero is the trick: a missing item starts at zero, so the first tea adds to nothing. After one pass, tea totals twenty-two point five and mug totals eight. The second algorithm finds the best line so far. We start by assuming the first line is best, then loop through all the lines, and replace best whenever a line has a higher total. After the loop, best holds the line with the biggest total, three teas at four point five. The third card shows a filter written both ways. The loop starts with an empty list, tests each line, and appends the item when the quantity is more than one. The comprehension below expresses the same thing in one expression, and now you can see how it maps: the loop's append value goes at the front, the for clause is the loop header, and the if clause is the test. So when should you use which? A comprehension suits one transformation or one filter. A loop is better when there are several steps, or a value carried from pass to pass, like the running totals. And remember that sum, min, and max already do common accumulations. Repeated logic is now visible. Next, we give it names, inputs, outputs, and clear responsibilities.

Until now, our order calculation has been a few lines we copy and change. A function packages those lines under a name so we can run them again with different inputs. You define one with def, a name, parameters in parentheses, and a colon, and then an indented body. Defining a function does not run it. The body runs only when you call the function, by writing its name with arguments in parentheses. An argument is the actual value you pass, and a parameter is the name that receives it. Look at the first function in the card. Calling line total with three and four point five binds qty to three and price to four point five, evaluates qty times price, and returns thirteen point five. The table traces those three steps. The word return sends a value back to the caller and ends the function immediately. Now the second function, which uses print instead of return. It shows thirteen point five on the screen, but it hands nothing back, so the name result is None. This is a very common beginner mistake: print displays a value to a person, and return gives a value to the program. A function with no return statement always returns None. A return can also sit inside an if, which ends the function early, and any lines after a return that has run never execute. The third function shows how to give back several results. Return min and max, separated by a comma, actually returns one tuple, and we unpack that tuple into low and high, two point two five and eight. Next, the different ways of passing arguments.

There are two main ways to pass arguments. A positional argument is matched to a parameter by its order, so line total of three and four point five gives qty three and price four point five. A keyword argument is matched by name, so you can pass price equals four point five and qty equals three in either order, and the result is the same. You can mix the two, but positional arguments must come first. Keywords make calls easier to read, especially when a function has many parameters, because the call explains itself. A wrong call raises a TypeError, and the message tells you why. Passing only one argument says a required argument is missing. Passing three says the function takes two but three were given. And passing qty both by position and by keyword says that it got multiple values for qty. Function definitions can also restrict how a parameter is passed. In the table, the signature is apply with price, a slash, rate, a star, and places. Parameters before the slash are positional-only, so the caller cannot pass price by name. Parameters after the bare star are keyword-only, so the caller must write places equals something. Parameters in between, like rate, accept either style. Keywords also help readers: apply of ten, zero point five, places equals zero explains itself, while a bare trailing zero does not. This is useful in a library, where you may want the freedom to rename a parameter later without breaking callers, or you want to force callers to name an easily confused option. Next, giving arguments default values.

A parameter can have a default value, written with an equals sign in the definition. If the caller omits that argument, Python uses the default, so price with tax of ten with a default rate of zero point five gives fifteen. A parameter with a default must come after those without one, or Python raises a SyntaxError. Now, a rule that surprises almost everyone: a default is evaluated once, when the def statement runs, not each time the function is called. For a number, that makes no difference. But if the default is a mutable object, such as an empty list, every call that uses the default shares that one list. Look at the first function in the card. The first call adds tea and returns a list holding tea. The second call adds mug, and returns tea and mug, because it is the same list. The second call sees the first call's item. The fix is shown below it. Make the default None, which cannot be changed, and then create a fresh list inside the function when the argument was not supplied. Now variadic parameters, which accept any number of arguments. A parameter with one star collects all the extra positional arguments into a tuple, so total of four point five and eight puts a tuple of two prices in prices. A parameter with two stars collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. In a full signature the order is ordinary parameters, then star args, then keyword-only parameters, then double-star kwargs. The stars also work the other way when calling: star in front of a list unpacks it into separate positional arguments, and two stars in front of a dictionary unpacks it into keyword arguments. Next, what really happens to an argument when a function receives it.

This section applies the name-and-object picture to function calls. When you call a function, each parameter becomes a new name for the very object you passed in. Nothing is copied. In the code card, order and p are names in the caller. Calling add coupon with order creates a second name, the parameter order, for the same dictionary. The diagram shows both names pointing at one dictionary. When the function assigns a coupon into it, it changes that shared object, so the caller sees the change. This is mutation. Appending to a list that was passed in works the same way. Now consider raise price. The parameter price is a new name for the float four point five. When the function runs price equals price times two, it does not change the float. Floats cannot be changed. It calculates a new float, nine, and makes the local name price refer to it. The caller's name p still refers to four point five. This is rebinding, and it affects only the local name. So the rule of thumb is simple. Mutating changes the object, and everyone who shares it sees the change. Assigning to a name changes only that name. There is one subtle pair to remember with lists: items plus-equals a list mutates the list in place, so the caller sees it, but items equals items plus a list builds a new list and rebinds the local name, so the caller sees nothing. Next, where Python looks when it meets a name.

A scope is the region of a program where a name is visible, and when Python meets a name, it searches four places in a fixed order, remembered as L, E, G, B. First the local scope, the names assigned inside the running function. Then the enclosing scope, which holds the names of any outer function that this function is nested inside. Then the global scope, the names at the top level of the file. And finally the built-in scope, which holds the names Python itself provides, like len, sum, and print. The code card shows it in action. Inside with tax, price and tax are local, but rate is not assigned there, so Python finds it in the global scope, and the function returns twelve. Local names vanish when the function returns, so asking for tax afterwards is a NameError. Now the trap in the second function. Reading a global from inside a function is fine, but assigning to a name inside a function makes that name local for the whole function. So count equals count plus one tries to read a local count that has no value yet, and Python raises an UnboundLocalError. A function nested inside another can read the outer function's names without any special syntax. There is a global statement that lets a function assign to a global, but it makes code hard to follow, and passing arguments and returning results is almost always clearer. One more hazard is shadowing. If you name a variable len, you hide the built-in function len, and a later call to len fails because the name now refers to a number. Next, why we prefer functions that depend only on what they are given.

A pure function has two properties. Its result depends only on its arguments, and it changes nothing outside itself. Anything else it does is called a side effect: printing to the screen, writing to a file, changing a list that the caller passed in, or changing a global variable. The table classifies four functions. With tax of price and rate is pure. Give it the same two arguments and you always get the same answer, and it changes nothing. With global rate looks harmless, and it does not change anything, but its answer depends on a hidden input, the global rate. The same call, with global rate of ten, could give twelve today and fifteen tomorrow, because someone changed the global. Passing rate as an explicit parameter makes the dependency visible at every call. Next, sort prices. It receives a list, sorts it in place, and returns None. Its side effect is that it changes the caller's list, and a caller who did not expect that gets a surprise. Compare it with the sorted built-in, which returns a new list and leaves the original alone. And the last row, printing a total, depends on its argument but writes to the screen, which is a side effect. Side effects are not bad, because a program that never prints or saves anything is useless. The point is to know where they are. A good habit is to keep calculations pure and push printing and file access to the edges of the program. Pure functions are easy to test, easy to reuse, and easy to reason about.

A function has a contract: what it expects, and what it promises. Python gives you three different tools to express it, and they do very different jobs. The first is a docstring, a string placed as the first line of the function body. It explains what the function does for readers. Python stores it, so the help function can show it, and it is available as the double-underscore doc attribute. The second tool is annotations. Writing colon int after a parameter and arrow float after the parameter list declares the types you intend. They are valuable documentation, and editors and type checkers read them, but Python itself does not enforce them. The proof is in the second function in the card: plain total is annotated to take an integer, yet calling it with the text ab and two runs without any complaint and returns abab, because text times a number repeats the text. The annotation did not stop it. The third tool is runtime validation, which is just ordinary code. If qty is less than zero, we raise a ValueError with a clear message. That check runs every time, and it is the only one of the three that actually rejects bad input. So use each for its purpose. Docstrings and annotations explain the contract to people and tools. Validation enforces it at runtime, at the places where untrusted data arrives. Where should you validate? At the boundaries, where untrusted data enters, such as user input or files. Inside trusted code, a clear docstring is usually enough. We will see more about raising and handling errors in the next chapter. Next, a function that calls itself.

Our product categories are nested: a category can have child categories, which can have children of their own. To total a whole category, we add its own total to the totals of all of its children, and each child does the same for its children. A function that calls itself like this is recursive. Every recursive function needs two parts. The base case is the situation where the function can answer directly without calling itself. For a category with no children, the loop body never runs, so the function returns its own total. The recursive case handles everything else by calling the function on each child, a smaller version of the same problem. The tree in the diagram is also the call trace. Calling category total on drinks first calls it on tea, which is a leaf and returns thirteen point five. Then on coffee, which calls it on espresso, a leaf that returns two point five, so coffee returns ten point five. Finally drinks adds zero, thirteen point five, and ten point five to return twenty-four. Each call has its own local total, so the calls do not interfere with each other. A recursive function with no base case calls itself forever, and Python stops it with a RecursionError. In CPython, the default limit is about one thousand nested calls, an implementation setting rather than a language rule. Anything recursive can also be written as a loop with an explicit stack of items still to visit. Recursion is usually clearer when the data is itself nested, and a loop is better when the depth could be very large. Next, we put functions together into a whole program.

Now we can organise a program. Decomposing means splitting it into small functions, each with one job. Our reporting program becomes four functions. Parse line turns a line of text into a tuple. Line total calculates the cost of one line. Order total adds up all the lines. And format report turns the total into text for the screen. Each function is small enough to understand, test, and reuse by itself, and only the last one has a side effect of showing something to a person. Here is something new that makes this even more powerful. In Python, a function is a value, an object like any other, so you can pass it to another function. Look at the sorted call in the code card. Line total, written without parentheses, is the function object itself. Adding parentheses would call it. Passing it as the key tells sorted to call line total on each sale and order the sales by the result. A function passed in to be called later is a callback. This finishes the key function preview from Chapter 2: now you can write your own. You can write your own functions that accept callbacks, too. Apply all takes a list of values and a function, and returns the result of calling that function on each value. The caller chooses the behaviour: pass tax and you get fifteen and thirty, pass str dot strip and you remove spaces. A good name says what a function returns or does, such as order total. Functions organise computation. Next, we connect that computation to files and handle failures at its boundaries.

Until now, our order data has lived inside the program. This chapter is about the boundary, where a program meets files, and the first thing to know is how to talk about where a file is. A path is the name of a location on disk, and the pathlib module gives it a Path object with useful methods. You build a path by joining parts with the slash operator, so Path of data, slash, orders dot csv, is the path to a file called orders dot csv inside a folder called data. Python uses the correct separator for your system, which means the same code works on Windows and on Linux. A relative path like this one starts from the current working directory, the folder the program was started from. When Python prints a path, you may see the name PosixPath or WindowsPath, depending on your system. That is the same object, just labelled for your platform. The table shows how a path comes apart. Name is the file name, stem is the name without its extension, suffix is the extension, and parent is the folder. With suffix returns a new path with a different extension, and leaves the original unchanged. Other methods ask questions without changing anything, such as exists and is file, or act on the disk, such as making a folder, listing files that match a pattern with glob, and reading or writing a whole small text file. If you read a file that is not there, Python raises a FileNotFoundError, which we will learn to handle later in this chapter. Next, what is actually inside a text file.

A file on disk does not contain characters. It contains bytes, which are numbers from zero to two hundred and fifty-five. So text has to be converted to bytes on the way out, which is called encoding, and converted back on the way in, which is decoding. Python keeps the two ideas as separate types. A str is text, a sequence of characters. A bytes object is raw data. They never mix, and trying to add one to the other raises a TypeError. The most common encoding is UTF-8, which can represent every character in Unicode. The table shows that one character can need between one and four bytes. The letter e is one byte, but e with an accent is two, so café has four characters but five bytes. Two Japanese characters need six bytes, and an emoji needs four. In the code card, we encode café and get the bytes c, a, f, and then two bytes for the accent. Decoding with UTF-8 gets the text back. Now the failures. Decoding the bytes with the wrong codec, here latin-1, does not raise anything. It quietly produces the wrong text, a capital A with a tilde followed by a copyright sign. That is the dangerous case, because nothing tells you. Other mismatches do raise, such as a UnicodeDecodeError when a byte is not valid in the encoding, and the exact wording of that message can vary between Python versions. Encoding text that the codec cannot represent, such as an accent into ASCII, raises a UnicodeEncodeError. The lesson is to always name the encoding when you open a file, and to use UTF-8 unless you know better. An errors setting of replace hides problems rather than fixing them, so use it only deliberately. Next, reading and writing files.

To work with a file, you open it. The open function takes a path, a mode, and, for text, an encoding, and gives back a file object. The mode decides what you may do, and the table lists the common ones. Read mode is the default. Write mode creates the file if it is missing, but if it exists, it empties it first, which is a destructive default worth remembering. Append mode keeps what is there and adds to the end. And x mode creates a new file but raises FileExistsError if the file is already present, which protects you from overwriting. The code card writes two lines to a file. Each call to write returns the number of characters written, ten for tea comma three comma four point five and a newline. Then we close the file, which flushes any pending data to disk and releases it. Then we reopen it for reading. Readline returns one line, including its trailing newline character. And a for loop over the file object gives the remaining lines one at a time, so we strip the newline before printing. Reading one line at a time matters for big files, because the program never needs the whole file in memory at once. The alternatives are read, which returns the whole file as one string, and readlines, which returns all lines as a list, and both are fine for small files. Binary modes, with a b, skip decoding and work with bytes. Notice how easy it would be to forget the close call. Next, a way to make that impossible.

Closing files by hand has two problems. First, it is easy to forget. Second, if an error occurs between open and close, the close line never runs. A file left open can lose data that was still buffered, and on some systems it stays locked. You might think Python will tidy up when the file object is no longer used, but when that happens is not something you can rely on, so it is not deterministic. The with statement solves it. You write with, then open, then as, and a name, and the indented block that follows can use the file. When the block ends, Python closes the file, and it does so whether the block finished normally or raised an exception. The code card shows both. The first with block reads and prints the lines, and afterwards f dot closed is True. The second raises a RuntimeError inside the block on purpose, catches it outside, and f dot closed is still True. The diagram shows the guarantee: after the file opens, the block either finishes or raises, and in both cases, the file ends up closed. You can open several files in one with statement, separated by commas, which is handy for copying from one file to another. And with is not only for files. Locks, database connections and temporary folders all use it to guarantee cleanup, and in Chapter 8 you will see how to write your own. From now on, every file in this course is opened with with. Next, two formats for structured data.

Two formats cover most structured data. The first is CSV, comma-separated values, the format a spreadsheet exports. The top card shows an orders file: a header row, then one order per line. The csv module's DictReader reads it and gives one dictionary per row, keyed by the column names from the header. Look at the first row in the code card. The quantity is the text three, not the number three, and the price is the text four point five. CSV has no types, so every value arrives as a string, and converting them is your job. Open the file with newline set to an empty string, so the reader can handle quoted fields that contain line breaks, and the writer in the same module adds quotes around any value that contains a comma. The second format is JSON, which is text that looks like Python dictionaries and lists. The loads function turns JSON text into Python objects, and dumps does the reverse. JSON keeps numbers as numbers, true and false as booleans, and null becomes None. But JSON has fewer types than Python, and the translation has limits. A tuple becomes a JSON array, so it comes back as a list. A dictionary key must be text, so an integer key comes back as a string. Sets, decimals, and dates have no JSON form at all, and dumps raises a TypeError, so you must convert them yourself first. For files, dump and load do the same job as dumps and loads but read and write a file object directly, and ensure ascii set to False keeps accented characters readable instead of escaping them. And malformed JSON raises a JSONDecodeError. Remember: parsing a format is not the same as validating the data. Next, what to do when something raises.

So far, an error has meant a traceback and a stopped program. An exception is an object that Python creates when something goes wrong, and it interrupts the normal flow until something handles it. You handle one with try and except. The code you suspect goes in the try block. If it raises an exception matching the except clause, Python skips the rest of the try block and runs the handler instead. Two more blocks complete the picture. Else runs only if nothing was raised, and finally runs always, even if a block ended with return. The function in the card has all four, and the table traces them. With the text three, the try completes, except is skipped, else runs and prints parsed, and finally prints done, then the function returns three. With the text x, the try stops at the int call, except runs and prints not a number, else is skipped, and finally still prints done. Notice that finally ran in both cases, which makes it the right place for cleanup. The most important habit is to catch narrowly. Name the exception you actually expect, such as ValueError, and use a tuple of names to handle more than one. A handler for the broad Exception class, or a bare except, will also swallow bugs you did not anticipate, such as a typo causing a NameError, and the program will carry on in a wrong state. Exceptions form a hierarchy. FileNotFoundError is a kind of OSError, and KeyError is a kind of LookupError, so a handler for the parent catches the child. Next, raising exceptions of our own.

You can raise an exception yourself with the raise statement. It stops the current function and unwinds through its callers, looking for a handler, exactly like the exceptions Python raises. Inside an except block, a bare raise re-raises the same exception, which is useful when you want to log something and then let the error continue. Often a low-level error is not meaningful to the caller. In our import, a ValueError from int says invalid literal for int, but it does not say which order was bad. So we catch it and raise a domain error, an error type named for the problem in our program. The class at the top of the card is a one-line pattern: it defines OrderError as a kind of ValueError, and we will explain classes properly in Chapter 7. The function catches the ValueError and raises an OrderError with a clear message naming the quantity and the order id. The key is the words from err. That records the original error as the cause, so Python prints both in the traceback, joined by the sentence: the above exception was the direct cause of the following exception. You see the low-level error and the meaningful one. If you raise a new exception inside an except block without from, Python still links the first one, as the context. And from None hides the original, which you should rarely want. A named error type has another advantage: callers can catch OrderError itself, instead of matching message text. Next, deciding what to do when a record is bad.

Data you did not write cannot be trusted, so you check it as it enters your program. The sample has three rows, each in a different state. The first is fine. The second has the text x as a quantity. And the third has a price of None, and this one deserves attention. When a CSV row has fewer values than the header has columns, the reader does not leave the key out. It fills the missing value with None. So catching a KeyError, which is the natural thing to do for a missing field, would miss it completely, and the None would travel on until some later calculation fails. Likewise, an empty cell is an empty string, which is a different thing from a missing value. The validator function in the card returns a list of every problem it finds in a row, not just the first, so a person fixing the file can correct everything in one pass. The messages name the field. Applied to the three rows, it gives an empty list for the good row, a quantity message for the second, and a price message for the third. Check more than the type: strip stray spaces first, remember that isdigit rejects negative and decimal text, and a quantity of zero may parse but still make no sense. Having found a problem, you must decide what to do, and the table lists four policies. You can stop at the first error, which suits situations where money must be right. You can skip the bad row and report it, which suits bulk imports, though someone has to read the report. You can substitute a default, which suits optional fields but can hide real gaps. And you can repair the value, which is only safe when the rule is certain. Decide the policy before the data arrives, and whichever you choose, count what you skipped. Next, two tricky kinds of values: time and money.

Two kinds of value look simple and are not: times and money. Start with time. A date is a calendar day. A datetime adds a time of day. The crucial distinction is between naive and aware. A naive datetime has no time zone, so nine thirty means nothing definite: nine thirty where? An aware datetime carries its zone. In the card, we create nine thirty in New York in October, then convert it to UTC and get thirteen thirty, because New York was four hours behind UTC at that date. Comparing a naive datetime with an aware one raises a TypeError, which is Python refusing to guess. The table shows how timestamp text is interpreted. Without an offset, the text is naive. Adding plus zero zero colon zero zero marks it as UTC, and minus four hours marks New York time, and thirteen thirty UTC is the same instant as nine thirty at minus four. The rule of thumb is to store and compare times in UTC, and convert to local time only to show someone. On some systems, the zone database may need installing separately. Now money. Floats cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, as zero point one plus zero point two reminded us. The decimal module can. Build a Decimal from a string, never from a float, because Decimal of the float zero point one faithfully copies the float's error, a long tail of digits. With strings, four point five zero times three is exactly thirteen point five zero. One more subtlety: Decimal's default rounding is half-even, which rounds a tie to the nearest even digit, so choose a rounding mode explicitly when money is involved. Next, one complete flow using everything in this chapter.

Now we put the chapter together. The input file has five orders. Two are valid, A one thousand one and A one thousand five. The others each fail differently: A one thousand two has the quantity x, A one thousand three has no price at all, and A one thousand four has the price abc. Read the program in the top card. It opens the file with a with statement, naming the encoding and setting newline, and reads it with DictReader. For each row, the try block converts the quantity with int and the price with Decimal, built from the string. The except clause is narrow. It names ValueError, which int raises for the x, TypeError, which Decimal raises for the missing price because the short row gave None, and InvalidOperation, which Decimal raises for abc. When one of these occurs, we record the order id and the name of the exception type. The else block runs only when the conversion worked, and it keeps the order id with the exact line total, the quantity times the price. After the loop, we add up the good amounts and print a report: one summary line with the counts and the total, and one line for each rejection. The terminal card shows the result: two valid, three rejected, a total of eighteen, which is thirteen point five zero plus four point five zero, and the reason for each rejection. Notice what we did not do: we did not crash on bad data, we did not silently skip it, and we did not use a float for money. This program does reading, validating, and reporting in one place, and it is getting crowded. The script now has several responsibilities. Next, we organise code and dependencies without relying on one large file.

The program from the last chapter is getting crowded. It reads, validates, calculates, and reports in one file. Python's answer is to split code across files, and every Python file is already a module. To use one module from another, you import it. In the card, calc dot py defines line total, and main dot py imports calc. When Python executes import calc for the first time, it finds the file, runs it from top to bottom, and binds the name calc to the resulting module object. Notice the print statement at the top of calc. It runs during the import, which is why we see loading calc, exactly once. The second import calc prints nothing, because Python remembers modules it has loaded in a dictionary called sys dot modules and reuses them. Everything calc defines lives in the module's own namespace, a private table of names. That is why we call calc dot line total, and why a name in calc cannot clash with a name in main. The table shows four ways to import. Import calc binds one name, calc. From calc import line total copies a single name into this module. Import calc as c is the same module under a shorter name. And from calc import star pulls in everything, which we avoid, because a reader can no longer tell where a name came from. Because top-level statements run at import time, a module should mostly contain definitions, not printing or real work. Finally, where does Python look? In the script's own folder first, then the standard library, then installed packages. So a file of yours named json dot py will hide the real json module, a surprisingly common mistake. Next, grouping modules into packages.

As a project grows, even a flat folder of modules gets hard to navigate. A package is a folder of modules that you import as a unit, usually marked by a file named init, with double underscores. Our reporting project is a package called orders, with modules calc, loader, and cli. The diagram is its import graph, where each arrow points from the module doing the importing to the module being imported. Cli uses calc and loader. And a file called main, with double underscores, lets us run the whole package. The init file runs when the package is first imported, and is often empty. There are two ways to write an import inside a package. An absolute import spells the full path from the package root, like from orders dot calc import line total. A relative import uses a dot to mean this package, as in from dot calc import line total, which says the calc module beside me. Relative imports only work inside a package, a point that matters in the next section. Now the classic problem. Suppose pricing imports from inventory, and inventory imports from pricing. Python starts loading pricing, which triggers loading inventory, which asks pricing for a name it has not defined yet, because pricing has not finished loading. The result is an ImportError saying it cannot import that name. The exact wording varies between Python versions, and newer ones may mention a partially initialized module and a likely circular import, but the symptom is the same: an ImportError between two of your own modules that import each other. The fix is to break the cycle. Move the shared code into a third module that both import. Or import the module itself, and look up the name when the function is called, by which time loading has finished. Next, how a module decides whether it is being run or imported.

Every module has a built-in name called double-underscore name. When Python runs a file as the program, that name is the text main. When the file is imported by another module, the name is the module's own path, such as orders dot cli. That small difference lets one file be both a library and a program. The bottom of the code card shows the pattern: if name equals main, then call main. Run the file, and main runs. Import it from somewhere else, and nothing runs, so importing has no side effects, and its functions are simply available. The table shows four ways to start the reporting program, and each one was run. First, python orders slash cli dot py. Python treats cli dot py as a lone script, with no parent package, so the relative import at its top fails with an ImportError. If the file used absolute imports instead, it would fail with a ModuleNotFoundError, because Python puts the script's own folder on the path, not the project's root folder. Second, python dash m orders dot cli. The dash m flag runs the module as part of its package, relative imports work, and it prints the total, twenty-one fifty. Third, python dash m orders runs the package's main file, which imports cli and calls main itself. In that case cli's name is orders dot cli, so its guard does not fire, and main file does the calling. And fourth, simply importing orders dot cli runs nothing yet, because the guard is false. Python also sets the package context for dash m, and you run it from the project root so the package can be found. Without a guard, top-level code runs every time the module is imported, which is almost never what you want. As a rule, start package code with dash m from the project root. Next, the modules that come with Python.

You already use the standard library: csv, json, pathlib, decimal, and datetime all came with Python. It is large, and you will never memorise it, so what matters is knowing how to find the right module. Start from the problem. The table groups modules by purpose. For data files, look at csv and json. For paths and copying files, pathlib and shutil. For dates and time zones, datetime and zoneinfo. For exact or statistical arithmetic, decimal and statistics. For counting and combining things, collections and itertools. And for matching and wrapping text, re and textwrap. Then explore from the prompt. In the code card, the statistics module gives us the mean of our three prices, four point nine one six six and so on, and the median, four point five. The built-in help function shows a function's documentation, and a module's double-underscore all list names its public functions and classes. Counter, from collections, counts items, so counting our order items, tea appears twice. Why prefer the standard library? It is tested, documented, and present on every installation, so your program runs anywhere Python does, without anything extra to install. Reach for a third-party package only when the standard one falls short. If an import fails with ModuleNotFoundError, either the package is not installed in this environment, or the name you used is not the name it is imported under, which is the subject of the next section. And remember last section's warning: a file of your own named like a standard module will hide it. Next, installing code that does not come with Python.

Libraries from outside the standard library are installed with a tool called pip, and that raises a problem. One project may need version one of a package, and another may need version two. If everything is installed in one place, they collide. The solution is a virtual environment: a folder containing its own copy of the installed packages, tied to a particular Python interpreter, the python program itself. The commands in the card are illustrations, and you do not need to run them. Python dash m venv dot venv creates an environment in a folder named dot venv. Activating it, with a command that differs on Windows, makes the python and pip commands in your terminal use that environment. Then python dash m pip install, followed by a name, installs a package into that environment only. Pip list shows what the environment contains, and a new one holds almost nothing. And pip freeze writes out the exact version of everything installed, which can be saved to a file. Many Linux systems also mark their own Python as managed by the operating system and refuse to install into it, which is another reason to use an environment. Now the source of much confusion, shown in the table. The name you give pip, the distribution, is not always the name you import. You pip install pillow but import PIL. You pip install scikit-learn but import sklearn, and you pip install beautifulsoup4 but import bs4. Keep the two ideas apart: the distribution is the thing you install, and the import package is the thing you use in code. Finally, an environment is disposable. It is not part of your source, so you never commit it, and you can delete and recreate it whenever you like. Next, how a project records what it needs.

Now we can describe the reporting project as three separate layers. The first is the source, your own code, here the orders package. The second is the declaration, a file named pyproject dot toml that says what the project is and what it needs. The third is the environment, the dot venv folder holding what is actually installed. The environment is generated, so it is never committed. The layout card shows the files and what each is for. In the second card, the pyproject file declares a distribution name, orders dash report, a version, and the Python versions the project supports. Notice that the distribution name differs from the import name, orders. It also lists dependencies. Here the entry is a range: python dash dateutil, greater than or equal to two point nine. A range says which versions are acceptable, so the project keeps working as new releases appear. A requirements file produced by pip freeze, by contrast, holds pins, written with double equals, an exact version that was tested. Together they let someone else reproduce your environment: create a fresh one, install the declared dependencies, and use the pins when you need exactly the versions you tested with. The deeper point is a boundary. Keep the code that calculates apart from the code that runs as a program, and keep the declaration apart from the installation. How a project is built and published, with a command-line entry point, comes in the last chapter. Modules organise code. Next, we decide when related data and behaviour should form domain objects.

So far, an order line has been a tuple or a dictionary. A class lets us define our own kind of object, with its own data and its own behaviour. A class is a blueprint, and an instance is one object built from that blueprint. In the code card, the class LineItem has one method, named init with double underscores, and it is the constructor. When we write LineItem of tea, three, four point five, Python does two things. It creates a new, empty LineItem object, and then it calls init, passing the new object as the first argument, which is conventionally named self. So self is the new instance itself. The three assignments store the item, the quantity, and the price as attributes on that instance, and together they are the instance's state. We read an attribute with a dot, so line dot qty is three. We can change one the same way, so line dot qty equals four updates it. The built-in vars function shows all of an instance's attributes as a dictionary. Python also lets you add attributes later, so a typo such as qyt instead of qty does not fail, it quietly creates a new attribute. Every instance has its own state, so creating a second line item for a mug does not affect the first. Is instance asks whether an object was built from a given class, and for our line it is True. Two mistakes are worth knowing. Forgetting an argument raises a TypeError naming the missing one, because init is an ordinary function with parameters. And asking for an attribute that was never set raises an AttributeError. The table collects the four words for this section: class, instance, attribute, and init. Next, where attributes live, and a very common surprise about sharing.

Data can live in two places. Instance attributes are set on self and belong to one object. Class attributes are written in the class body, outside any method, and belong to the class, so every instance shares them. When you read an attribute, Python searches in order: first the instance's own attributes, then the class. That is why a constant such as a tax rate, defined once on the class, can be read through any instance. But if you assign through an instance, you do not change the class value. You create a new instance attribute that hides it. The card shows the mistake that follows from this. The class Basket has items equals an empty list in its body, which is a class attribute, so there is exactly one list. The add method appends to self dot items, which finds that one list through the class. So after a adds tea, the second basket b also contains tea, and vars of a is empty, because nothing was ever stored on the instance. The diagram shows both names reaching the same list. This is the class version of the mutable default trap from Chapter 4, and the fix is the same idea: create the list in init, so every instance gets its own. A quieter trap involves numbers. If a class has count equals zero and a method does self dot count plus-equals one, Python reads the class value, adds one, and stores the result as a new instance attribute. After two calls, the instance says two, and the class still says zero. If you want a counter shared by everyone, update it through the class name. Next, what a method really is.

A method is simply a function defined inside a class. Look at total in the code card. It has one parameter, self, and when we write line dot total, Python passes line as that first argument. The table shows exactly what Python runs: line dot total is the same as LineItem dot total with line passed in. Once you see that, self stops being magic. It is just the first argument, which Python fills in for you. Call the method on the class without an instance and you get a TypeError, because self is missing. The second kind is a class method. The line above it begins with an at sign, which marks a decorator. We will explain exactly how decorators work in Chapter 9, so for now read it as a label that changes how the function below it behaves. A class method receives the class itself, conventionally named cls, instead of an instance. The classic use is an alternative constructor. From text takes a string like tea comma three comma four point five, splits it, converts the pieces, and returns cls of those values, a new instance. Because it uses cls rather than the name LineItem, a subclass that inherits it gets an instance of the subclass back. The third kind is a static method, which receives neither self nor cls. It is just an ordinary function that lives in the class's namespace because it belongs with the class conceptually, such as checking whether a quantity is valid. Two mistakes: defining a method without self, so that calling it on an instance raises a TypeError complaining about the extra argument, and calling an instance method on the class without passing an instance. Most of your methods will be ordinary instance methods. Reach for a class method when you need a different way to build an instance, and a static method rarely. Next, a shortcut for classes that mostly hold data.

Writing init by hand for every data-holding class is repetitive. The dataclass module removes the repetition. You put at-dataclass above the class and list the fields with annotations, and that decorator reads them and writes the methods for you. Again, we will see exactly how a decorator works in Chapter 9. The version of LineItem in the card has no init at all, yet LineItem of tea, three, four point five works, and it prints as LineItem, with item equals tea and so on, because a readable repr was generated too. A third generated method, eq, makes two instances equal when all their fields are equal, which a plain class would not do. The table lists what is written. Adding frozen equals True makes instances immutable, so assigning to a field raises a FrozenInstanceError, and a frozen instance can be used as a dictionary key. Now the per-instance default. If a field needs a list, you cannot write lines colon list equals an empty list. A dataclass refuses, raising a ValueError that says the mutable default is not allowed, because that one list would be shared, exactly as in the last section. Instead you write field with default factory equals list, which calls list afresh for each instance. Two notes. The annotations name the fields, but nothing checks the types, so a string in an int field is accepted. And the replace function makes a modified copy of an instance, which is useful with frozen ones. Next, building bigger objects from smaller ones.

Real programs are made of objects that work together. Composition is the simplest way: one object holds other objects. In the card, an Order has a list of lines, set up in init, and each line is a LineItem. We say an Order has line items, a has-a relationship. Now look at the responsibilities.
