A LineItem knows how to compute its own total from its quantity and price. An Order knows how to add a line and how to total the whole order, but it does not know how a line does its arithmetic. Order dot total asks each line for its total and adds the answers up. The diagram shows that: the order asks tea, which answers thirteen point five, and asks mug, which answers eight, so the order reports twenty-one point five. This is collaboration, and the design principle behind it is that one class should not reach inside another's fields. If the order calculated quantity times price itself, then changing how a line is priced, say adding a discount, would mean changing the order too. Because it asks the line for its total, the order is untouched when a line changes. A second benefit is testing: each class can be tested alone. So when should you use composition? Whenever one object contains or uses another, which is most of the time. It is also the safer default over inheritance, which we meet next, unless the relationship is genuinely an is-a relationship.

Sometimes one kind of object really is a special case of another. A bulk line item is a line item, with a discount. Inheritance expresses that. In the card, the class BulkLineItem names LineItem in parentheses, so it inherits everything LineItem has: the init, and the total method. It then overrides total by defining its own method with the same name. Inside the override, super dot total calls the parent's version, so we reuse the basic calculation and then apply a ten percent discount if the quantity is at least ten. For ten teas at four point five, the base is forty-five, and the answer is forty point five. For three teas there is no discount. How does Python find a method? It searches a fixed list of classes, called the method resolution order. For a bulk line item, that is BulkLineItem first, then LineItem, then object, the class that every class ultimately inherits from. The diagram shows that chain, and you can see it with the dunder mro attribute. When a class has several parents, Python computes the order following consistent rules, so a method is never found in two places by accident. Two ways to check relationships: is instance is True for a subclass instance, while asking for the exact type with type of b is LineItem is False. And super follows the method resolution order rather than simply meaning the parent, so with a class D inheriting from B and then C, a call chain visits D, then B, then C, then their shared parent. Now two cautions. If you override init in a subclass and forget to call super dot init, the parent's setup never runs, and the object lacks attributes, leading to an AttributeError later. And inherit only when the relationship is truly is-a. A bulk line item is a line item, so it is a good fit. An Order is not a line item, so it holds them instead. Next, using different objects through the same call.

Polymorphism means one call can do different things depending on the object. We have three pricing strategies, written as three small classes: PerUnit charges four point five each, Bulk takes ten percent off at ten or more, and Flat charges twenty regardless. They are unrelated classes. They share no parent, only a method name, price. The function order cost takes a strategy and a quantity and simply calls strategy dot price of quantity. It never asks what kind of strategy it received. The table shows the three answers for three items and for ten. This works because of duck typing, from the saying: if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, treat it as a duck. Python does not check an object's type before a call. It looks for the method when the call happens, so any object with a price method works. That makes code flexible: to add a new strategy, you write a new class, and order cost needs no change. The failure mode is that a wrong object is discovered late. Passing the text tea raises an AttributeError, saying the string has no attribute price, but only when order cost runs. Passing the class itself instead of an instance fails differently, with a TypeError about a missing argument, because price was called without a self. The design lesson is that the caller depends on a behaviour, not on a type. Python's built-ins work this way too: len accepts anything that has a length. Next, deciding what rules a class must protect, and when not to use a class at all.

An invariant is a rule that must always be true for an object, such as a line item's quantity being positive. The best protection is to make a bad object impossible to create. In the card, the line item is a frozen dataclass with a post init method, which runs right after the generated init. If the quantity is not positive, it raises a ValueError with a clear message. So the first call builds a line, and the second, with a quantity of zero, is refused before any bad object exists. Because the class is frozen, nobody can change the quantity later to something invalid. Methods can protect invariants too. An order's add method can check that it is given a line item, and raise a TypeError otherwise. But be honest about the limits. By convention, a name starting with an underscore, like underscore lines, means internal, hands off. Python does not enforce that. Code that reaches in and appends a string to the list can still break the order, and the failure shows up later, far from the cause. In the next chapter, you will see properties, which can enforce rules on attribute access. The last question is whether to write a class at all. The table gives a guide. A single calculation with no stored state is best as a function. Fixed fields with little behaviour suit a dataclass or a tuple. State that must stay valid across calls suits a class that guards it. And interchangeable behaviours can be functions or small classes. Validate at the boundary where data enters, and trusted objects can rely on their invariants. Objects now model the domain. Next, we connect their behaviour to the protocols used by Python's own syntax and built-ins.

In Chapter 3, a for loop worked on lists, strings, dictionaries, and ranges, and it did not matter which. This chapter explains what makes that possible. The answer is a pair of protocols, which are agreements about which special methods an object provides. An iterable is anything with an iter method that returns an iterator. An iterator is an object with a next method that returns the next value, and raises StopIteration when there are no more. The built-in functions iter and next call those methods. The code card does it by hand. We ask a list for an iterator, then call next. We get three, then five, and then the third call raises StopIteration. That exception is not an error. It is the signal that the loop uses to stop quietly. So a for loop does this: it calls iter once, then calls next repeatedly until StopIteration. Now notice what happens afterwards. Listing the same iterator again gives an empty list, because an iterator is used up. It does not rewind. That is the difference in the table. A list is iterable, but it is not an iterator, so asking a list for an iterator gives you a fresh one each time, which is why you can loop over a list as often as you like. An iterator's own iter method returns itself. You can write your own. Our Countdown class has an iter method that returns self, and a next method that counts down and raises StopIteration at zero. Because Countdown is its own iterator, it is one-shot too. If you ask for an iterator from something that has none, such as an integer, Python raises a TypeError saying it is not iterable. Next, a much easier way to write iterators.

Writing a class with next and iter for every iterator is tedious. A generator function is a shortcut. Any function that contains the word yield is a generator function. When you call it, the body does not run. You get back a generator object, which is an iterator. The code card prints as it runs so you can see exactly what happens. Creating the generator prints nothing. The first call to next runs the body from the top, prints start, enters the loop, prints yield one, and reaches the yield statement. There it pauses, handing back the value A one thousand one. The function's local variables, and the exact place where it stopped, are kept. The second call to next resumes right after the yield, goes round the loop, prints yield two, and pauses again with A one thousand two. The third call resumes, the loop ends, done is printed, the body finishes, and Python raises StopIteration. The table traces those four steps. Why use a generator? Because it produces values on demand. Nothing builds a whole list in memory, and a generator can even be infinite, such as one that yields Fibonacci numbers forever, because the consumer only asks for as many as it needs. For simple cases, there is a one-line form called a generator expression. It looks like a list comprehension but with parentheses. Summing the line totals needs no extra brackets, so sum of q times p for each line gives twenty-one point five without ever building a list. Like every iterator, a generator can be consumed only once, and its close method stops it early. Next, chaining generators into lazy pipelines.

Generators become powerful when you chain them. In the card, read rows yields lines of text one at a time, and parse takes any iterable of rows and yields them split into pieces. Both print as they work. We connect them by passing one to the other, and nothing happens at all yet, because nothing has asked for a value. Now watch the two calls to next. The first one asks parse for a value. Parse asks read rows for a row, which prints read tea and yields it. Parse prints parse tea, and yields the split row. So each item travels through every stage before the next item is even read. Only then does the second next call read mug. The work is interleaved, one item at a time, instead of reading all the rows and then parsing all the rows. That is lazy evaluation. The table contrasts it with eager evaluation, where a list comprehension does all the work up front and keeps every result in memory. Laziness saves memory, can work with endless sources, and does only the work that is needed. The price is that a generator is one-shot. In the second example, listing the totals gives thirteen point five and eight, and listing the same generator again gives an empty list, because it was already consumed. If you need to loop twice, keep a list. The itertools module is a toolbox of lazy building blocks. Count produces endless numbers, islice takes a slice from any iterator, chain joins iterables, accumulate gives running totals, pairwise gives neighbouring pairs, and batched groups items in fixed sizes. Groupby groups only neighbouring equal items, so sort first. Next, guaranteeing cleanup.

In Chapter 5, we used with to close files and promised to explain how it works. Now we can. A context manager is any object with two special methods. When a with statement starts, Python calls the object's enter method, and whatever it returns is bound to the name after as. When the block ends, however it ends, Python calls exit. Look at the class in the first card. Enter prints open and returns the object itself. Exit prints close. So running the with block prints open orders, then using orders, then close orders. And if the block raises an error, exit still runs, and it receives the exception's type, value, and traceback as arguments. Its return value matters. Returning False lets the exception continue on its way, which is what you almost always want. Returning True would hide the exception, a power to use rarely and carefully. Writing a class for this is verbose, so the standard library offers a shortcut. The contextmanager decorator, from the contextlib module, turns a generator function into a context manager. Everything before the yield is setup, the yielded value is bound by as, and the code after the yield, in a finally block, is cleanup that runs even if the block raises. This is the generator form in the second card, and it does exactly what the class does. The contextlib module also has ready-made managers. Suppress ignores one named exception. Redirect stdout captures printing into a buffer. And ExitStack manages a variable number of resources, closing them in reverse order. Next, what it means for two objects to be the same.

There are two different questions you can ask about two objects. Are they equal, meaning do they have the same value? And are they the same object? Double equals asks the first, and calls the object's eq method. The is operator asks the second. A plain class has no eq of its own, so it is equal only to itself. Dictionaries and sets need a third thing: a hash, a whole number computed from an object, used to find it quickly. They rely on a contract. If two objects are equal, they must have equal hashes. Python helps. The moment you define eq on a class without defining a hash method, Python sets the hash to None, and the class becomes unhashable. The first line of the card shows the TypeError. Adding a hash method that hashes the same data that eq compares restores it, and now equal keys find each other: the lookup returns a. The second half of the contract is that a hash must never change while the object is in use as a key. Look at the last lines. We put a key in a dictionary, then mutate it. The dictionary stored the entry under the old hash, so a lookup using the old value finds the right place but no longer matches, and a lookup with the new value looks in the wrong place. The entry is lost, and a KeyError is raised either way. That is why dictionary keys should be immutable: strings, tuples, or frozen dataclasses. The table summarises the types we know. Lists are unhashable. Dataclasses are unhashable unless frozen. And one subtle example of the contract at work: one equals one point zero, and their hashes match, so a dictionary lookup with a float finds an integer key. Next, how objects present themselves.

An object can present itself in two ways, and Python gives you a special method for each. The repr method is for programmers. It should be unambiguous, and ideally look like the code that would recreate the object, such as LineItem of tea, three, four point five. The str method is for end users, and it can be friendlier, like three times tea. If you define only repr, str falls back to it, but not the other way round. Which one is used where? Print, str, and f-strings use str. The interactive prompt, the repr function, and anything displayed inside a container use repr. The card shows it: asking for the list that holds our line item displays the repr, because a list shows its items by repr. Another special method controls truth testing. When you write if x, or call bool, Python first tries the bool method. If there is none, it tries len, and a length of zero means false. If neither exists, the object is true. That explains why empty containers are false, and why our line item with a quantity of zero can be made false by defining bool. Python also gives you tools to inspect any object. Dir lists its attribute names, vars shows the instance dictionary, type gives its class, and hasattr, getattr with a default, and callable ask questions about it. A good habit is to always write a repr, because it makes debugging, logging, and error messages readable, instead of showing an unhelpful object at some memory address. Next, making our own classes behave like built-in ones.

Nearly all of Python's syntax is a call to a special method, and that is what lets your classes behave like built-in ones. Take containers first. Our Order class defines only two methods: len, which returns the number of lines, and getitem, which returns a line by index. With just those two, a surprising amount works. The len function works, and square brackets work, including negative indexes. And so do for loops, the in operator, list, and max, because Python can fall back on getitem with the numbers zero, one, two, and so on until it fails. Defining iter and contains makes these operations more direct, but they are optional here. Operators work the same way. When Python sees a plus b, it calls a dot add of b. The Money class in the second card defines add so that it adds cents. It also checks the type of the other operand, and if it is not Money, it returns NotImplemented, which is a special value, not an exception. That tells Python: I do not know how to do this. Python then tries the other operand's reflected method, and if that fails too, it raises the familiar TypeError, unsupported operand types. So Money plus five fails cleanly. Cooperation has details. Three times a money value needs the reflected multiply method, rmul, because the integer does not know about Money. And the sum function starts from the integer zero, so it would try zero plus Money and fail. You must pass a start value, Money of zero, and then the answer is three cents. Next, controlling attribute access.

In Chapter 7, we said an underscore only means keep out, and that Python cannot enforce a rule on plain attributes. Properties can. A property looks like an attribute from the outside, but runs code on access. In the card, qty is defined as a property with a getter, which just returns the stored value, and a setter, which checks the new value and raises a ValueError unless it is positive, and only then stores it. The stored value lives under the name underscore qty, so the property and the storage do not clash. Notice the line in init. Self dot qty equals qty looks like a plain assignment, but it goes through the setter, so even the constructor cannot create an invalid line item. The table shows the effects. Assigning zero raises the ValueError. A second property, total, has no setter and is computed each time from the quantity and price, and you read it without parentheses. Trying to assign to it raises an AttributeError saying the property has no setter. And the instance dictionary shows underscore qty, not qty. How does this work? A property is an example of a descriptor, which is an object stored on the class that defines get and set methods. When you read or write an attribute with that name, Python calls those methods instead of touching the instance dictionary. You can write your own descriptors, but properties cover almost every case. A separate hook, getattr, is a fallback that runs only when a name is not found at all. As a rule, start with plain attributes, and add a property only when a rule or a computation appears. Next, when objects disappear.

The last topic in this chapter is when objects stop existing. An object lives as long as something refers to it. In CPython, the standard interpreter, each object keeps a count of its references. The sys dot getrefcount function reads it, and it reports one more than you might expect, because passing the object to the function creates a temporary reference. So a list with one name shows two, and with a second name, three. When the count reaches zero, CPython frees the object immediately. The card demonstrates it with a class whose del method prints a message. Creating one and deleting its only name prints del one at once. But be clear: this immediate behaviour is a detail of CPython, not a promise made by the Python language, and other implementations free objects differently. Reference counting has a weakness. Two objects that refer to each other, a cycle, keep each other's counts above zero. In the card, deleting both names prints nothing, and the two objects linger until CPython's cycle collector, run here by calling gc dot collect, finds them and prints del two and del three. The del method is a poor place for cleanup, because the language does not guarantee when, or even whether, it runs. A weak reference lets you refer to an object without keeping it alive, and it returns None once the object is gone. The table separates what you can rely on from what you cannot. Counts reaching zero and the cycle collector are CPython details, and when del runs is not guaranteed. What is guaranteed is your own code: with blocks and explicit close calls run exactly when you say. So never depend on garbage collection to release a file or a lock. Protocols let objects cooperate. Next, we use functions themselves as composable objects and make interfaces more explicit.

In Chapter 4, we learned that a function is an object, and that you can pass line total to sorted as a key. This chapter builds on that. Because a function is a value, you can do anything with it that you can do with a value. In the first card, we put a function, a lambda, and the built-in string method strip into a dictionary, and call the one we want by name. We can pass functions to other functions, which is what a callback is, and we can return them from functions, which the next section uses. You have met lambda in passing, and now we can define it. A lambda is a small unnamed function. Lambda v colon v times two takes a value and returns it doubled. It is limited to a single expression, so it cannot contain statements, and an assignment inside one is a SyntaxError. And it has no real name: its name is the text lambda in angle brackets, which is unhelpful when you read a traceback. So use lambdas for one-off keys and callbacks, as in the max call that finds the biggest line, and write a proper def whenever the function deserves a name or needs more than one expression. Python has another kind of callable. Any object whose class defines the call method can be called like a function. The Rate class stores a rate when it is created, and each instance, called with a price, applies it. So a callable object is a function that also carries state. The table compares four kinds: a def function, a lambda, a callable object, and a closure, which we meet next. The built-in callable function tells you whether you can call something. A good callback has a clear contract about what it receives and returns, so name it well and document it. Next, functions that remember where they were created.

In Chapter 4, you met the enclosing scope: the names of an outer function. Now we use it. When a function is defined inside another and uses one of the outer function's names, Python keeps that name alive for as long as the inner function exists. That inner function is a closure. In the card, make tax of zero point five returns the inner function with tax, and with tax remembers the rate. Calling make tax again with zero point two returns a separate closure that has its own rate, which is why the two calls give fifteen and twelve. A closure can also carry changing state. Make counter keeps a count, and each hit increments it. But assigning to a captured name creates a new local one unless you declare it with nonlocal, which is why the version without nonlocal fails with an UnboundLocalError, as it did in Chapter 4. Each counter has its own count, so a second counter starts again at one. Mutating a captured list needs no nonlocal, because we change the object rather than assign the name. Now the most famous closure trap, in the second card. We build three lambdas in a loop, each returning i. Calling them gives two, two, two, not zero, one, two. A closure keeps the name i, not its value at the moment the lambda was created, so all three look up the same variable, which by the time we call them holds its final value, two. This is called late binding. There are three standard repairs. Give the lambda a default argument, i equals i, which captures the current value at creation time. Or use functools dot partial to fix the argument. Or write a small factory function that takes i as a parameter, so each lambda gets its own. Next, functions that wrap other functions.

We have used decorators since Chapter 7, with at-property, at-classmethod, and at-dataclass, and each time we said we would explain them later. Now we can. A decorator is just a function that takes a function and returns a replacement. The at sign is shorthand. Writing at log calls above a def means exactly: define line total, then assign line total equals log calls of line total. The decorator in the first card defines a wrapper function that accepts any arguments, prints, calls the original with the same arguments, prints the result, and returns it. After decoration, calling line total runs the wrapper, which is why it prints calling line total and returned thirteen point five. At property and at dataclass work the same way. Decorators can be stacked, and then the order matters. The one nearest the def is applied first, so it is the innermost layer. The second card uses a tag decorator. With b on top and i underneath, the result is b wrapped around i wrapped around hi. Swap them, and the tags nest the other way round. A parameterised decorator takes arguments, as in at tag of b. Here, tag is not the decorator but a factory that returns the decorator, so you need three nested layers: the factory takes the argument, the decorator takes the function, and the wrapper takes the call's arguments. And a very common mistake is to use a factory without parentheses, writing at repeat. Python then passes the function to the factory instead, and the first call to the result fails with a TypeError about a missing argument. One cost to know about: a wrapper replaces the original function, so its name and docstring are lost. The next section shows the fix. Next, the standard tools for functions.

The functools module collects the standard tools for working with functions, and three of them matter most here. The first fixes the cost of decorators from the last section. A decorated function is really the wrapper, so its name is wrapper and its signature is just star a and star star k, which breaks help, debugging, and error messages. Placing at functools dot wraps of fn above the wrapper copies the name, the docstring, and the signature from the original, and records the original as the dunder wrapped attribute. Always use it. The second tool is partial. Partial of price with, zero point five, creates a new function with the first argument already filled in, so calling it with ten gives fifteen. It is often cleaner than a small lambda. The third is caching. Putting at functools dot cache on a function makes Python remember each result, keyed by the arguments, so a repeated call returns instantly without recomputing. That is excellent for a slow, repeatable calculation, such as a recursive Fibonacci. The lru cache variant keeps only the most recent results up to a size you choose, evicting the oldest. Cache info reports hits and misses. But caching has two limits, shown in the second card. The arguments must be hashable, so passing a list raises a TypeError, just like a dictionary key. And the function must be pure. Here, with rate reads a global. The first call returns fifteen. We then change the global rate, and the second call still returns fifteen, a stale answer, because the cache never looked at the global. The right answer would be twenty. So cache only functions whose result depends solely on their arguments. Next, describing types without enforcing them.

Chapter 4 said that annotations are documentation that Python does not enforce. This section shows what they are for. A type alias gives a type a descriptive name. In Python three point twelve and later, the type statement does it: type Price equals float, and then type Line as a tuple of a string, an integer, and a Price. The signature of total can then say it takes a list of Line and returns a Price, which reads like documentation. Generics describe how types relate. First of T, in square brackets, is a function whose result type follows its input: give it a list of integers and the result is an integer, give it a list of strings and the result is a string. A generic class, like Box of T, holds one kind of thing. Protocols connect to what you learned about duck typing in Chapter 7. The Priced protocol declares a price method, and any object with a matching method fits it, with no shared parent, so it writes the duck typing down in a form that tools can read. Now the vital point, shown in the table. A static type checker is a separate tool that reads your hints before the program runs and reports mismatches. Python itself does not enforce them. Calling g with a string, where an integer is declared, runs until the arithmetic inside fails. A function annotated to return a string can return an integer, and nothing complains. Passing an object without a price method fails with an AttributeError, but only when the call happens. And checking a protocol with isinstance works only if you mark it runtime checkable, and then it checks only that the methods exist. No particular checker is required for this course. So treat hints as a contract for readers and tools, and keep runtime validation for the boundaries where untrusted data enters. Next, choosing between all these tools.

We now have many ways to choose which code runs, so this section is about choosing between them. Take the three pricing rules from earlier chapters. The first option is a dictionary of functions, mapping each pricing name to its function. Looking up the function and calling it is a single line, new cases are added by registering a function, and an unknown name raises a KeyError. The second option is an if chain or a match statement, which keeps every case visible in one place, and a final default case can raise a clear error for unknown input. The third option is singledispatch from functools. It chooses the function by the type of the first argument. We register a float formatter and a list formatter, and the right one runs: three point one four one five nine becomes three point one four, and a list becomes its items formatted and joined. Other types fall back to the default. A decorator can also build a registry, like the command decorator that records each function in a dictionary under a name. Use classes when behaviour carries state, as in Chapter 7. The table matches situations to tools. But notice the last point, and the most important. Every layer of abstraction is something else for a reader to understand, test, and debug. A pricing function that always charges the same way needs none of these. Write the direct code first. Add a dictionary, a decorator, or a class when you have two real cases that differ, not one hypothetical case that might someday appear. Code is now composable. Next, we decide how independently waiting or computing work should execute.

Programs often have to do several things at once, and two words describe different ideas. Concurrency means several tasks are in progress at the same time, even if only one is actually executing at any instant. Parallelism means several tasks are genuinely running at the same instant, on separate processor cores. You can have concurrency without parallelism: one cook can have several dishes underway, switching between them while something simmers. Which approach helps depends on what the work spends its time doing. I O bound work spends most of its time waiting: for a network reply, a disk, or a database. CPU bound work spends its time computing, such as hashing, parsing, or number crunching. The code card measures the first kind. The function wait sleeps for two tenths of a second, standing in for a network call. Running four of them one after another takes eight tenths of a second. Running them in four threads takes two tenths, because the waits overlap, and a waiting thread is not using the processor. Now the second kind. Four calls of a function that does heavy arithmetic took about the same time in four threads as in a plain loop. That result was measured on a GIL-enabled build of CPython three point thirteen with four cores, and section eight explains why it depends on the build. The table keys the choice to where time goes. Waiting favours threads or async. Computing needs more than one core doing real work at once. And a tiny task can cost more to hand off than to run, so overlap does not help. All the figures here are rounded and vary between runs and machines, so the habit to take away is to measure with your own workload. Next, threads and what they share.

A thread is a path of execution inside a single process, and every thread in a process shares the same memory. That makes sharing data easy, and it is also the source of the main danger. You start a thread with Thread, giving it a target function and arguments, call start, and later call join to wait for it to finish. If a thread raises an exception, Python prints the traceback, but only that thread ends. The main program carries on, so you must collect results and errors deliberately. A daemon thread is one that Python abandons when the program exits. Now the hazard. The statement counter plus-equals one looks like one step, but it is three: read the value, add one, write it back. The table traces two threads. Thread A reads zero. Thread B also reads zero. Thread A writes one. Thread B writes one. Two increments happened, but the counter says one. An update was lost. In the first run I forced a thread switch between the read and the write, and two threads each adding two hundred ended near two hundred and one, not four hundred. The exact number changes each run, which is the nature of a race condition: the result depends on timing. The fix is coordination. A lock lets only one thread into a protected section at a time, so the read, add, and write cannot be interleaved. The same test with a lock gave four hundred. An event lets one thread wait until another signals it. And thread local storage gives each thread its own private value. The responsibility for all of this is yours: threads share memory, and nothing protects it automatically. Next, processes, which do not share it.

A process is an independent running program with its own memory. Two processes share nothing by default, which removes the shared memory hazards of threads, but it creates a different problem: moving data between them. When you give a process pool a function and arguments, Python pickles them, converts them to bytes, sends those bytes to the worker, and the worker unpickles them. Results travel back the same way. The code card shows it working. The function square is defined at the top level, so a worker can import it by name, and mapping it over five numbers returns zero, one, four, nine, and sixteen. Notice the if name equals main guard. On platforms where workers are started fresh, each worker imports your module, and without that guard it would start workers of its own. Now see what cannot cross the boundary. A lambda cannot be pickled by name, so submitting one fails with an AttributeError saying it can't get the local object. A lock is tied to the process that owns it, so pickling one raises a TypeError. Functions defined inside other functions fail the same way. The table compares threads and processes. Memory is shared for threads and separate for processes. Data crosses by reference for threads, but is pickled both ways for processes. A crashing thread can take the whole program down, while other processes survive a crashed worker. Starting workers and copying data cost time, which I could not turn into a general number, since it depends on the start method and the data, so measure for your workload. On a standard GIL build, processes are how CPU-bound Python code uses several cores. The default way of starting a worker differs between platforms and Python versions, and it was fork on the machine used here. Next, a friendlier interface to threads and processes.

Managing threads and processes by hand gets tedious, so the standard library provides executors. An executor owns a pool of workers and takes work from you. The same interface covers both a thread pool and a process pool, so you can often switch by changing one name. You hand over work with submit, giving a function and its arguments, and it returns a Future immediately. A future is a handle to work in progress: the answer may not exist yet. Calling result on it waits until the work finishes, then returns the value, or re-raises the exception the function raised. So errors in a worker are not lost: they surface where you collect the result. There are three common ways to collect. Results one at a time with result. In order of completion, using as completed, which gave fast, then mid, then slow even though slow was submitted first. Or in submission order, using the executor's map method, which gave a, b, c. With map, if one item failed, the error appears when you reach that item. The table lists what else a future can tell you. Asking for a result with a timeout raises TimeoutError if it is not ready, but the work itself carries on. Cancel succeeds only for work that has not started yet: a queued future was cancelled, and a running one was not. Using the executor in a with block waits for submitted work and shuts the pool down, and submitting after shutdown raises a RuntimeError. Everything so far uses extra threads or processes. Next, a different model that uses neither for waiting.

Async programming is a different way to overlap waiting, using one thread. A function defined with async def is a coroutine function. Calling it does not run the body. It returns a coroutine object, a suspended computation, and nothing happens until something awaits it or schedules it. An event loop runs the coroutines, on a single thread. The key idea is cooperative scheduling. A coroutine runs until it reaches an await, and there it voluntarily hands control back to the loop, which can run another coroutine in the meantime. The first call in the card awaits fetch a, and then fetch b, one after another, so it takes four tenths of a second. Passing both to gather lets the loop start both, and while each is waiting, the loop runs the other, so it takes two tenths. This is concurrency without parallelism and without any extra thread. It also means the loop is only as responsive as its least cooperative coroutine. The table measures that. A ticker coroutine wakes four times, every fifty milliseconds. While another coroutine awaits a sleep, the ticks arrive about when expected. But when the other coroutine calls the ordinary blocking time dot sleep, the whole loop freezes, and the ticks slip to zero, three tenths, and then later. So never call blocking functions inside a coroutine. If you must, asyncio dot to thread runs a function in a worker thread and lets you await it. Two pitfalls. Calling a coroutine without awaiting it does nothing: the program carries on, perhaps with only a warning, and the work never happens. And asyncio dot run starts the loop, so calling it from inside a running loop raises a RuntimeError. Next, controlling and stopping async work.

Starting async work is easy. Stopping it cleanly is the hard part, and Python gives you structured tools. A task group, from asyncio dot TaskGroup, owns the tasks created inside it, and the async with block does not finish until all of them are done. If one task fails, the group cancels its siblings, waits for them to clean up, and then raises the errors together as an ExceptionGroup, which you catch with except star. The code card shows exactly the order that printed: job two failed, so its cleanup ran, job one was cancelled, and then job one's cleanup ran. Cancellation works by raising a CancelledError inside the task at its current await. That means a task can clean up in a finally block, and the card's job prints its cleanup either way. The convention is to re-raise CancelledError, so cancellation completes. The table lists a surprise: if a task catches CancelledError and does not re-raise it, the task simply finishes, and the cancellation is ignored. In the run, the task printed swallowed and then returned finished anyway. Timeouts use the same mechanism. Asyncio dot timeout cancels the block when time runs out, and raises a TimeoutError, after the inner cleanup has run. Shield is the opposite: an outer timeout cancelled only the shield, and the inner task was still running and finished normally afterwards. And gather needs care. Without return exceptions, it raises the first error to you but leaves the other tasks running, which can surprise you, while return exceptions equals True hands every outcome back as a value. These tools need Python three point eleven or later. Next, sharing state safely, and not overloading things.

We saw a lost update in section two. Here is the honest complication. I ran the plain counter plus-equals one in four threads, two hundred thousand times each, with no lock, and the total was exactly eight hundred thousand. It did not fail on that run. That does not make it safe. The statement compiles to separate steps: load the global, load the number, add, and store the result, and a thread switch can land between any of them. Whether it does depends on timing, the build, and the version, so a passing run proves nothing, and nothing in the language prevents a bad interleaving. The table groups the situations. A read, modify, write sequence is not guaranteed safe. A single list append showed no lost items in forty thousand, but that is an implementation behaviour, not a promise to rely on. A queue between threads is safe, because it locks internally, and state owned by a single thread is safe because nothing is shared. So the habits are: hold a lock around read-modify-write sequences, pass data through queues, and prefer data owned by one thread. The second idea is bounding work. Without limits, a fast producer can pile up work faster than a slow consumer handles it, using unlimited memory. A queue with a maximum size fixes that. When it is full, put waits, or fails with queue dot Full if you give a timeout or use put no wait. This is called backpressure: a slow consumer slows the producer down. A bounded semaphore limits how many workers may be inside a section at once. Six threads were started, and the peak number inside was two. Async code has the same tools, with an async queue and an async semaphore. Next, why all of this depends on which Python you run.

We can now explain the result from section one, where CPU-heavy work gained nothing from threads. CPython, the standard implementation, has a global interpreter lock, the GIL. Only one thread at a time may run Python bytecode, so threads doing computation take turns instead of running in parallel. A waiting thread releases the lock, which is why threads still help I O bound work, as we measured. The GIL is a detail of CPython, not part of the Python language. Other implementations make different choices, and the language definition does not promise it. Recent versions of CPython can also be built as free-threaded builds, without the GIL, where CPU-bound threads can run in parallel on separate cores. You can ask which kind you have. In the card, sysconfig dot get config var of Py GIL disabled is False, and sys dot is gil enabled is True, so the machine used for this course ran a GIL-enabled build. That is important: I could not measure a free-threaded build, so I make no claim about how much faster it is. Treat any speedup figure with suspicion until you have measured it on your own workload. According to CPython's documentation, which I could not run here, a free-threaded build can also switch the GIL back on, for instance if you load a C extension that has not declared support for running without it, so extension compatibility matters. The table sums it up. With the GIL, CPU-bound threads run one at a time. Without it, they can run in parallel. In both cases, I O bound threads overlap while waiting. And the practical advice is to test on the build you will deploy, and keep your locks. A missing GIL does not make shared state safe. It makes unsafe code fail more often. We now have a toolbox of execution models, and each adds complexity. Next, we combine correctness, diagnosis, performance, and distribution into one coherent program.

Until now, we have checked our code by running it and looking at the output. A test automates that. It runs code on a known input and compares the result with what you expect, and it keeps running every time the code changes. The card shows tests for our pricing code written with unittest, which ships with Python. A test class extends TestCase, and every method whose name starts with test is a test. Good tests cover three things. Typical cases, such as three items at four fifty giving thirteen fifty. Boundaries, such as a quantity of zero, or an empty order. And failures, where the right behaviour is to raise an error, which assertRaises checks. The last class is a regression test. A regression is a bug that returns after being fixed, and a regression test pins the correct behaviour so it cannot come back unnoticed. The terminal card shows a real run. The discount function treated a percentage of ten as a fraction, so it computed one minus ten, and the test failed with a report showing Decimal minus one hundred eighty against the expected eighteen. The report points straight at the bug. After we fixed the function to divide by one hundred, all six tests passed and the run ended with OK. One practical lesson from setting this up: test discovery failed with an ImportError until the tests folder contained a file named init, because discovery needs it to be a package. Floating-point results need assert almost equal, because zero point one plus zero point two does not equal zero point three. And tests should be isolated from the outside world. A temporary folder gives each test its own files, and mock dot patch replaces a real dependency with a stand-in. These are annotated examples for you to read, and nothing here asks you to submit or be graded. Next, what to do when a program fails and you do not yet know why.

Fixing a failure is a skill, and the best habit is a method rather than guessing. First, reproduce it, with the smallest input you can find that still fails. Second, read the traceback, starting from the last line, which names the error, and then reading upward to the line in your own code where it stopped. Third, form a hypothesis about the cause and check it, with a print statement, a debugger, or a test. And fourth, fix it, and add a regression test so it stays fixed. The card shows a function that averages a list. Calling it with an empty list fails with ZeroDivisionError, division by zero, and the last line of the traceback says so. Python's debugger, pdb, makes checking a hypothesis easy. Running the script with python dash m pdb stops at an uncaught exception in what is called post-mortem mode, showing the file, the line, and the function where it failed, and then you can inspect values. Typing p, then a name, prints that value, so you can see that the list is empty and the total is zero. The table lists the commands: n runs the next line, s steps into a call, c continues, w shows where you are in the call stack, l lists nearby code, and q quits. The breakpoint function placed in your code stops there on purpose. An assertion is a check written for programmers. The assert statement raises an AssertionError with your message if its condition is false, which documents an assumption and catches your own mistakes early. But it has a limit: running Python with the dash capital O flag removes every assertion, so never use assert to validate user input or anything that must hold in production. For that, raise a real exception, as in Chapter 5. Next, recording what a running program does.

A print statement shows a value, but it has no level, no timestamp, and no way to be switched off without editing code. The logging module records events with a level, a source, and a message, and lets you control what is shown from one place. There are five levels, with numbers: debug, ten, for detail useful when diagnosing; info, twenty, for normal milestones; warning, thirty, when something is odd but the program continues; error, forty, when an operation failed; and critical, fifty, when the program cannot continue. You set a threshold, and anything below it is dropped. In the card, the program is configured at info, so the debug message is not shown, the info message about reading five rows is, and so is the warning about the rejected row. Choose the level by who needs to notice the event, not by how you feel about it. Each module gets a logger of its own, named for the module, such as orders dot import. Logger names form a hierarchy with dots, so setting the level on orders affects everything beneath it. Configure the output once, at your program's entry point, with basic config, and have libraries only create loggers. How you write a record matters. Pass values as arguments after a message with percent placeholders, rather than building the string yourself. And a caution I confirmed: an expression you pass as an argument is still evaluated even if the level is switched off, so avoid expensive calculations inside a debug call. The exception method, used inside an except block, records the message and the full traceback at error level. Most important is context. A warning that says row A one thousand two was rejected, with the reason, can be acted on, while one that says bad data cannot. Next, finding out why a program is slow.

Before making a program faster, find out where the time goes, because intuition about performance is often wrong. To time a small snippet, the timeit module runs it many times and reports the total in seconds. Running it several times with repeat, and taking the minimum, gives the figure least disturbed by whatever else the computer was doing. To time a section of a larger program, call time dot perf counter before and after. To find which parts of a whole program are slow, use a profiler. The cProfile module records every function call and how long it took. The card shows the result for a small program that calls a slow function five times and a fast one a hundred times. The columns are in the table. N calls is how many times a function ran. Tot time is the time spent inside the function itself, excluding what it called. Cum time is cumulative, including everything it called. In this run, the generator expression ran a million and five times, which is exact and repeatable, while the seconds, about a third of a second in total, are specific to this machine and this run. Notice how the profile answers a question: nearly all the time is under slow, and inside it, in summing a generator of a million items, so that is where an improvement would count. Two cautions. Profiling itself slows a program, so compare the share of time each function takes, not the absolute totals. And always record a baseline measurement before changing anything, then measure again afterwards, so you know whether the change helped. Next, why some choices are fast and some are not.

Complexity describes how the cost of an operation grows as the data grows, and it explains why some collection choices from earlier chapters matter. Take membership. Asking whether a value is in a list makes Python compare the items one by one, so the cost grows with the length of the list. Asking whether a value is in a set, or whether a key is in a dictionary, uses hashing and takes about the same time however large the collection is. I measured it with a two hundred thousand item collection, looking for the last item, and the set was more than a hundred times faster. That is the real reason to prefer a set for many lookups. Adding and removing differ too. Appending to a list is cheap, but inserting at the front shifts every other item along, so it grows with the length. A deque, from the collections module, is cheap at both ends. Counting shows the cost of a nested pattern. Calling count on the list for each distinct word scans the list again every time, roughly n times n, while a Counter makes one pass, and in the test it was clearly faster. Memory has trade-offs too. A list stores every item, so its size grows with its length, while a range stores no items at all, and a generator keeps only its current state, so it stays small however many values it will produce. The byte counts in the card are what CPython three point thirteen reported, such as fifty-six bytes for an empty list. They are implementation details and will differ between versions, so use them to compare, not as promises. The advice is the same as before: choose the right structure first, measure when it matters, and do not optimise code that is not a bottleneck. Next, code that handles data it does not control.

Everything that comes from outside your program is untrusted: files, network data, command-line arguments, and what people type. The rule that protects you is to treat it as data, never as code, and the card shows three places where that rule is broken. First, deserialization. The pickle format can rebuild almost any Python object, and that includes calling functions while it loads. The example class tells pickle to call print, and loading the bytes printed code ran during unpickle. Here it was harmless, but a malicious payload could run anything the loading program may do. So never unpickle untrusted data. Use json for data, or ast literal eval for plain Python literals, which refuses anything else, as the failed call showed. Calling eval or exec on text has the same problem. Second, running other programs. With shell equals True and text from a user, a semicolon inside the text starts a second command: the output showed report and then INJECTED, two commands. Passing a list of arguments with no shell treats the whole text as one argument, and the output was a single line. The subprocess run function also has check equals True, which raises CalledProcessError when the program exits with a non-zero status, instead of silently carrying on. Third, paths. A file name supplied by a user can contain dot dot slash to climb out of the folder you intended. Resolving the path and checking that it is still inside your base folder, as in the last line, catches that. Two final habits: use the secrets module, not random, for anything security related, and keep passwords out of source code and logs. These are defensive examples that only touch local, harmless data. Next, turning a script into a real command.

A command-line interface is the layer that turns what a person types into a call to your code. The argparse module, in the standard library, builds one from a description. In the card, build parser creates the parser with a program name and a description. The first argument, path, has no dashes, so it is a required positional argument. Tax starts with two dashes, so it is an optional option. We give it a type of float, so argparse converts the text for us, and a default. Currency uses choices, which limits it to US dollars or euros, and verbose uses store true to make a flag that is false unless given. Argparse writes the help text for you, so asking for help prints a usage line and describes every argument. The table shows what each kind of invocation did, and I ran every one. A complete command runs, with the defaults filled in for options not given. A missing path, a tax of lots, and a currency of pounds each print the usage line and a specific error, and exit with status two. Exit status matters because other programs use it: zero means success, and any other number means failure. At the bottom of the file, sys dot exit of main passes the returned status back to the shell. One design point makes everything easier to test. Main takes the arguments as a parameter that defaults to None, which means use the real command line. A test can call main with a list of arguments directly, with no terminal involved. Keep the real work in ordinary functions, such as those from earlier chapters, and keep the parser thin. Now the boundaries around a project. There are three. The source is your own files. A build turns a pyproject dot toml declaration into a wheel, a ready-to-install file, or a source distribution. And installation puts a built package into an environment, where a project scripts entry maps a command name to your main function, so the command exists. Keeping the three apart tells you what to commit, what to generate, and what to delete and recreate. Next, putting the whole program together and packaging it.

Now we bring the whole course together on the reporting tool. In Chapter 6, we organised the code into a package. In Chapter 5, we validated rows and used exact decimal money. In this chapter, we added tests, logging, an understanding of performance, safe handling of untrusted input, and a command-line interface. The last step is packaging, so that someone else can install the tool and run a command. The top card is a pyproject dot toml file, like the declaration from Chapter 6, now with three additions. A build system section says which tool builds the project, here setuptools. The project section names it, gives a version, and states the oldest Python it supports, here three point ten, which is the version I verified against and not the Python used to write it. And a project scripts section maps the command name orders dash report to the function main in the cli module, which tells installers to create that command. The terminal card is an illustration of a local run that I actually performed in a throwaway folder. Building produced a wheel, a ready-to-install file, and also a source distribution. I installed the wheel into a fresh virtual environment. The installed command ran, printing that it would read the file with a tax of zero point two, and exited with status zero, and importing the package reported version zero point one point zero. Uninstalling removed the command again. One honest detail: the first build failed, because the older setuptools packaged with this system was not compatible with its Python, so I installed a current setuptools into a scratch environment, which is an environment problem and not a flaw in the project. Publishing the package, and deploying it to servers, are outside this course. You can now read, organise, test, diagnose, and package a Python program.
